newsitem.title: USA: Hot, humid weather aids Minnesota crop development.
newsitem.headline: Hot, humid weather aids Minnesota crop development.

text.p: Heat and humidity helped crops in Minnesota to develop quickly in the week ended Sunday, said the state's Agricultural Statistics Service.
The report noted however that "excessive rainfall and strong windstorms left much of the state hoping for some drier and calmer days."
Corn height gained 16 inches during the week to reach an average of 59 inches, exceeding the height a year ago by three inches and surpassing the five-year average by six inches.
Average soybean height was 17 inches, the same as the five-year average for the date. Forty-four percent of soybeans were blooming, also in line with the five-year average.
"Root rot and other problems related to wetness have been showing up in some soybean fields," the report noted.
Soil moisture was rated one percent very short, six percent short, 67 percent adequate and 26 percent surplus.
"Some localities were bypassed by recent storms and are still in a short soil moisture situation. However, problems arising from having more than enough water are more prevalent," the report noted.
Eighteen percent of spring wheat was turning ripe, versus a five-year average of 27 percent.
